title: Yara and the Well
premise: Urban explorer Elodie Almeida breaks into the abandoned Almeida family homestead—her own inherited property, though she's spent years pretending otherwise—and finds a hand-dug well shaft connecting to tunnels absent from every municipal survey. The house's mirrors lag one second behind reality, and in that stolen second, something else moves. As Elodie traces the tunnels, they learn their grandmother taught the town a lullaby whose final verse was cut out to seal a bargain: the well keeps its dead quiet as long as no one sings it whole. When a vengeful descendant of the well's original victims begins performing the verse at town gatherings, the dead start surfacing, and Elodie must decide whether loyalty to the family name is worth the truth of what the Almeidas did. In the end, Elodie sings the last verse alone at the well's mouth—not to seal the dead away, but to free them—collapsing the tunnels and shattering every mirror, finally choosing justice over inheritance.
about_author: Lior Nystrom is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade documenting structures that official maps insisted didn't exist. They write horror about places that remember more than the people who lived in them.

chapters.title: Off the Survey
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. An urban explorer with a grudge against her own surname, Elodie breaks into the derelict Almeida homestead to map its cellar for an anonymous client. She finds a sealed hatch behind the cistern and a hand-dug shaft dropping into tunnels no survey acknowledges. The beat is cold competence curdling into unease: she knows this house better than she admits.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Camping overnight to document the shaft, Elodie notices the hallway mirror reflecting her movements a full second late—and in that second, the reflection keeps moving after she stops. She films it; the footage shows nothing wrong. The emotional beat is the first crack in her disbelief: she doesn't believe, but she starts taking notes.

chapters.title: The Verse That Was Cut
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, intercut with grandmother Maren's 1962 journal entries. In the attic, Elodie finds sheet music for a local lullaby with the last verse physically razored out, and Maren's diary describing 'the arrangement' made after the well 'got loud' in 1931. The beat is dread through documentation: the horror has paperwork.

chapters.title: The Man Who Sings
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Following the tunnels under town, Elodie encounters Corvin Ashe, a gaunt man performing the lullaby's missing verse outside the church hall while listeners walk away weeping without knowing why. He recognizes her name—Almeida—and smiles. The beat is exposure: staying invisible was never an option, because someone has been waiting for an Almeida.

chapters.title: What the Well Was For
chapters.summary: Maren's journal, 1931–1934, read by Elodie. The entries reveal the Almeidas drowned striking miners in the well and bought the town's silence with the song: the verse sung whole keeps the dead asleep; unsung, they wake angry. Elodie realizes the mirrors aren't haunting her—they're buffering her from what's already rising. The beat is complicity: her inheritance is a crime scene.

chapters.title: Lag
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Back at the house, every reflective surface now runs two seconds late, and the reflections have begun arriving before she does—showing her things she hasn't done yet: standing at the well's mouth, singing. Corvin leaves a note on her windshield: 'Your grandmother owed them a verse.' The beat is hunted inevitability.

chapters.title: Descendants
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Elodie and Corvin. Corvin's chapters reveal he is the great-grandson of a miner left in the well, raised on the song as a weapon, and he intends to sing the verse at the founders' day gathering until the dead take their accounting. Elodie tries to warn him the waking won't distinguish victims from heirs. The beat is two grievances pointed at the same wound.

chapters.title: Founders' Day
chapters.summary: Corvin's POV, then Elodie's. At the town gathering, Corvin begins the final verse before the assembled descendants of both families; the temperature drops, mirrors across the square fog over, and the ground hums. Elodie tackles him mid-line, and the half-sung verse hangs unfinished over the crowd like a held breath. The beat is catastrophe interrupted, not prevented.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The tunnels are open now; the dead surface nightly, and the town turns on the Almeida name. Elodie descends to the well carrying Maren's journal as testimony, understanding that sealing the song again would just restart the debt. She must finish what Corvin started—but on her terms. The beat is resolve: choosing truth over the family's survival-by-silence.

chapters.title: Sung Whole
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the well's mouth, Elodie reads the victims' names aloud from the journal, then sings the last verse entire—not as a lock, but as a release. The dead pass upward like heat off stone, the tunnels collapse, and every mirror in the house catches up to the present all at once before cracking. Epilogue: the surveys now show the tunnels, empty. The beat is costly peace: justice rendered outside any law, and an heir who gave the inheritance back.
